questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify who gains and who loses from a policy change
questions.stem: A cartographer's projection sheet asks which households should be shaded as winners when a new bus fare structure lowers the cost of travel for most riders and raises it for a small group of daily commuters.

options.text: The households whose cost falls and the households whose cost rises, shown separately
Only the households whose cost rises, since a distributional effect concerns losses
options.misconception: reads a distributional effect as being only about losses

options.text: Only the households whose cost falls, since a distributional effect concerns gains
options.misconception: reads a distributional effect as being only about gains

options.text: All households on the route, since the service as a whole has improved
options.misconception: treats an overall improvement as erasing who bears the cost

questions.explanation: A distributional effect is read by asking who gains and who loses, which requires shading both sides of the change separately. Showing only one side or treating the service as a whole conceals the incidence of the policy.
questions.hint: You need both sides of the change marked.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a single indicator can mislead about policy success
questions.stem: In a projection note, explain why a single headline measure of success can give a misleading picture of a policy's results.

answer.exemplar: A single measure compresses a policy's aims into one figure and so leaves out whatever the figure does not capture. A scheme that promises lower costs, better service and faster delivery may show an excellent figure on cost while service quality falls, and the aggregate will still look like success. Because the chosen indicator also fixes what counts, the party being measured can shift effort towards whatever the indicator rewards and away from what it ignores, so the measure eventually records its own side effects. Reporting a small set of complementary measures, each tied to a distinct aim, avoids both the omission and the distortion.

questions.explanation: The item tests why one headline number cannot stand for a policy with several aims, since it hides whatever it does not count. It also invites the measurement to be gamed once the reward attached to it is clear.
questions.hint: Ask what the chosen figure leaves out.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish public attention from the government agenda

stimulus.body: A survey annotation records that the issue drawing the most correspondence from the public was the state of the riverside path, while the government's published programme of work for the year contained nothing about it and instead devoted most of its entries to a business tax review.

questions.stem: According to the annotation, what does the contrast between correspondence and the published programme show?

options.text: Public attention and the official agenda matched, since the tax review matters to most correspondents
options.misconception: assumes the agenda matches what correspondents raised

options.text: Public attention and the official agenda diverged, since the issue most raised by citizens was absent from the government's priorities
The government had noticed the riverside issue, since correspondence is always a sign of official awareness
options.misconception: treats correspondence as proof of official awareness

options.text: The correspondence measure is unusable, since letters are written only by the most committed citizens
options.misconception: dismisses correspondence as written only by the committed

questions.explanation: The annotation shows a divergence between what citizens raise and what the government has scheduled, which is the standard gap between public attention and the official agenda. Attention on its own does not move a government agenda, and the correspondence figure is a rough but usable signal.
questions.hint: Compare the two lists rather than either one alone.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Delivery left out of a promise
questions.learningObjective: Identify the gap between a policy announcement and its delivery

stimulus.body: A margin note on the projected sheet records that the scheme was announced with a target of opening twenty new clinics within two years, that three opened in the first year, and that the official programme lists the announcement under the heading of things delivered.

questions.stem: According to the margin note, what has gone wrong?

options.text: The official programme is wrong to list the scheme at all, since partial progress is not worth recording
options.misconception: treats partial progress as not worth recording at all

options.text: The target was set too low, since three clinics is a reasonable first year for any scheme
options.misconception: blames the modest target rather than the record of delivery

options.text: The announcement has been counted as delivery, so a promise of twenty clinics is being reported as though it were met
The clinics opened early, so the programme is running ahead of the promise
options.misconception: reads partial delivery as running ahead of the promise

questions.explanation: Listing an announcement under delivered work treats the making of a promise as the meeting of it, which hides the gap between the target and the three clinics actually opened. Partial progress is worth recording, but it must be recorded as partial.
questions.hint: Ask what the heading actually measures.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the sequence of implementation steps matters
questions.stem: The projection notes argue that a scheme which trains staff before installing new systems succeeds, while the same scheme run the other way fails. Which explanation best fits that pattern?

options.text: Training always takes longer than installation, so the order made no difference
options.misconception: attributes the outcome to step duration rather than order

options.text: The staff were more willing in the first version because of better management practice
options.misconception: blames staff willingness rather than the sequence of steps

options.text: Installing systems is always a waste of money, so the second scheme could never have worked
options.misconception: treats installing new systems as inherently wasteful

options.text: Early steps shape what later steps are possible, so sequencing determines whether the scheme can be absorbed

questions.explanation: Implementation is path dependent, since each step changes the state that the next step encounters, and staff who have not been trained are poorly placed to use the new systems. The pattern is explained by that dependence rather than by any preference of the staff.
questions.hint: Ask what state the second step finds the first one left behind.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a policy produces identifiable winners and losers
questions.stem: The legend drafted for the projected map must explain why a subsidy produces both a visible group of beneficiaries and a less visible group who end up paying.

options.text: Because subsidies are always paid for by taxation, so the cost falls on taxpayers as a group
options.misconception: assumes subsidies are always paid for by taxation

options.text: Because the subsidy raises demand for a scarce good, so its cost is spread across all users of that good
Because the scheme exempts a category of users from a charge that others continue to pay
options.misconception: confuses a subsidy with a charge exemption for a group

options.text: Because political decisions distribute benefits and costs unevenly by design
options.misconception: explains the hidden payers as a matter of political design

questions.explanation: The direct beneficiaries are easy to identify, but the cost appears as a higher price caused by increased demand, and that price is paid by every user including the beneficiaries themselves, which makes the losers far less visible. The exemption framing would apply to a different kind of policy entirely.
questions.hint: Ask how the subsidy reaches the non-beneficiaries.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the two efficacy forms can diverge
questions.stem: Explain, in a projection note, how political efficacy can rise on one dimension while falling on the other.

answer.exemplar: Internal efficacy concerns whether a person believes they can affect political outcomes, and external efficacy concerns whether the political system responds to people like them. The two can move in opposite directions when experience changes one without changing the other. People who join campaigns and see their own effort produce a visible result grow in internal efficacy, while watching government ignore every request they have made reduces external efficacy. A survey that reported only the rising figure would record growing political confidence and would miss the growing sense that the system does not listen.

questions.explanation: The item tests that the two forms are separate beliefs that can move independently, and that reporting only one conceals the divergence. Political engagement can raise confidence in one's own voice while lowering faith in the system's responsiveness.
questions.hint: Ask which belief the campaign changed.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply disaggregation to locate a failing dimension

stimulus.body: A survey annotation records a programme scored on four dimensions, with an overall mark that looked satisfactory. On inspection, the marks for reach, for cost and for speed were all strong, while the mark for take-up was the lowest in the whole survey and had fallen for three years running.

questions.stem: According to the annotation, what does disaggregation of the overall mark reveal?

options.text: The programme has failed on every dimension, since a low take-up mark invalidates the other scores
options.misconception: lets one weak dimension invalidate the other scores

options.text: All four dimensions are satisfactory, since a satisfactory overall mark settles the question
options.misconception: treats a good overall mark as settling every dimension

options.text: Three dimensions carry the average while take-up is failing and deteriorating, which the single mark conceals
The overall mark should be replaced by the single weakest dimension, since one figure must be reported
options.misconception: proposes replacing the aggregate with its weakest component

questions.explanation: Separating the dimensions shows that the overall figure was propped up by three strong scores while take-up was both weak and falling, which is exactly the failure the aggregate concealed. Substituting the weakest dimension for the aggregate would destroy the information the other three dimensions carry.
questions.hint: Break the overall mark back into its parts.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish stated intent from actual incidence

stimulus.body: A margin note records that a levy was introduced to fund repairs to a footbridge in one district, that the money was described as coming from the owners of large vehicles in the district, and that in the first year the charge fell mainly on small firms that used the same route daily while large vehicle owners used a diversion.

questions.stem: According to the margin note, what does the contrast show?

options.text: The diversion was unlawful, since only the charged vehicles may use the original route
options.misconception: treats lawful rerouting as unlawful avoidance of the charge

options.text: The levy worked as intended, since the revenue came from large vehicle owners as described
options.misconception: takes the stated design as the actual incidence

options.text: The levy was too low, since small firms complained more loudly than the owners
options.misconception: reads complaint volume as the size of the charge

options.text: The incidence differed from the intent, because the vehicles that rerouted avoided the charge that smaller users could not

questions.explanation: The stated design charged large vehicle owners, but those able to reroute avoided the charge while smaller users with no alternative bore it, so the burden landed elsewhere than intended. Intent describes the design, while incidence describes where the burden actually fell.
questions.hint: Who actually paid, as against who was named?

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the design of a composite success measure
questions.stem: A programme reports one success figure that averages cost, speed, coverage and quality. Which criticism is best founded?

options.text: Averaging is invalid because the four dimensions are measured on different scales
options.misconception: objects to averaging on grounds of mixed measurement scales

options.text: Averaging lets a strong result on one dimension offset a failure on another, so the figure should be reported with its parts
The figure is the right approach because it gives decision-makers a single number to act on
options.misconception: justifies a single figure by the need for one number

options.text: The figure cannot be criticised, since composite measures are standard practice
options.misconception: treats standard practice as exempt from criticism

questions.explanation: An average is a useful summary but it allows gains on one dimension to cancel failures on another, and the cancellation is invisible in the total. Reporting the composite alongside its components lets a reader see which dimension is carrying the result.
questions.hint: Ask whether a failure can hide inside the total.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why attention does not translate into priority
questions.stem: A survey legend shades the issue attracting most public attention, and the government agenda shades a different issue entirely.

options.text: Attention is irrelevant, since only the official agenda is worth plotting
options.misconception: dismisses public attention as not worth plotting

options.text: Attention and priority are the same, since what people discuss must be what governments do
options.misconception: assumes attention and priority are the same thing

options.text: Attention and priority are distinct, since attention reflects salience while priority reflects choice and capacity
Priority follows attention automatically, once the media have reported an issue widely
options.misconception: believes media coverage converts attention into priority

questions.explanation: Public attention measures how salient an issue feels, while an agenda reflects what the government has chosen and can deliver, and the two routinely diverge. Treating attention as automatically decisive mistakes a measure of salience for a decision.
questions.hint: Ask what the government chose, as against what people raised.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Delivery left out of a promise
questions.learningObjective: Explain why announcements are recorded as achievements
questions.stem: Explain, for the projection note, why an official record of achievements tends to contain more announcements than deliveries.

answer.exemplar: An announcement is produced quickly and visibly by a single decision, while a delivery depends on other bodies, on budget approvals and on procurement, and takes far longer. Officials are also judged on what they can show, and an announcement is presentable at once whereas a delivery only appears once it is finished. If the record counts both as achievements, then the report rises whenever announcements rise, which teaches the wrong lesson to the officials who read it. The corrective is to keep two separate columns, one for commitments made and one for commitments met, and to report the ratio between them.

questions.explanation: The item tests why a record built on announcements drifts away from outcomes, because announcements are easier to produce and easier to count. Keeping commitments and deliveries in separate columns exposes the gap.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two is quicker and easier to show.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a first implementation step constrains later ones

stimulus.body: A survey annotation records that a housing programme began by relocating households already on the waiting list into the first new units, which meant every later unit had to be filled with people already known to the programme, and that the households who had been given priority on grounds of need waited until the second phase.

questions.stem: According to the annotation, what effect did the first step have?

options.text: It had no effect, since the waiting list was fixed before the programme began
options.misconception: claims the first allocation step changed nothing

options.text: It improved fairness, since early tenants could then be asked for their views on the design
options.misconception: reads the first allocations as an improvement in fairness

options.text: It reduced costs, since the first units were filled without an eligibility check
options.misconception: credits the first allocations with saving money

options.text: It fixed the order of the queue, so the earliest units went to those already in the system rather than to those in greatest need

questions.explanation: Once the first units went to people already in the system, the programme's own allocation pattern became fixed and the households with the strongest claim waited for the second phase. The first step did not merely happen before the others, it determined them.
questions.hint: Ask what the first allocations locked in.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how concentrating benefits builds support for a policy

stimulus.body: A field note records that when a change was designed so that a single union would gain substantially and the costs were spread thinly across many small employers, the change passed. When a later attempt spread the benefit more widely, it failed. The note asks whether the pattern is about support or about numbers.

questions.stem: According to the field note, what explains the pattern?

options.text: Numbers decide, since a change benefiting more people always wins
options.misconception: assumes the number of beneficiaries decides the outcome

options.text: Concentrating the benefit on a well organised group concentrates support, which is what carries a change through
The union's membership decided it, since it voted the measure through
options.misconception: attributes the outcome to the union's own vote

options.text: The costs were too high, since employers could not afford them in either version
options.misconception: blames the size of the costs for the outcome

questions.explanation: A concentrated and organised beneficiary can mobilise support that a broadly and thinly spread benefit cannot, so concentrating the gain is often what makes a change passable. The number of beneficiaries is not the same thing as the strength of the support they can generate.
questions.hint: Ask where the organised support came from.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a report that shows rising political confidence
questions.stem: A survey shows participation rising and internal efficacy rising, while external efficacy falls sharply. Which reading is best founded?

options.text: The system is becoming more responsive, since people feel more capable of influencing it
options.misconception: reads personal confidence as system responsiveness

options.text: Engagement is failing, since rising participation shows people have lost faith in the system
options.misconception: reads rising participation as lost faith in the system

options.text: People are engaging more confidently while becoming more convinced that engagement does not change anything
The survey is unreliable, since the two forms of efficacy never move in opposite directions
options.misconception: denies that the two efficacy forms can diverge

questions.explanation: Participation and internal efficacy both rose, which indicates growing capacity and willingness to act, while falling external efficacy indicates a growing belief that the system will not respond. The two dimensions are separate, so an inverse movement is a substantive finding rather than a data problem.
questions.hint: Read each measure against the belief it actually captures.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a composite score needs its components reported
questions.stem: A projection legend shows an overall grade for each district, and one district grades middling overall while grading worst in the whole survey on reliability of the service.

options.text: Reliability does not belong in the grade, since the other components matter more
options.misconception: proposes dropping the failing component from the grade

options.text: The overall grade is wrong, since the worst component should always determine it
options.misconception: believes the weakest component should set the composite

options.text: The grade shows the district is uniformly mediocre, since middling is the definition of average
options.misconception: reads a middling composite as uniform mediocrity

options.text: The overall grade hides a serious weakness, because the other components offset the failing one

questions.explanation: Because a composite allows strong components to offset weak ones, the middling grade conceals a dimension that is the worst in the survey. The components must be published alongside the grade for the weakness to be visible.
questions.hint: Ask what the other components are doing to the average.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why aggregate totals conceal distributional effects
questions.stem: Explain, for the projection note, why an aggregate total can rise while the situation of most households worsens.

answer.exemplar: An aggregate records a single total for the whole population, so it moves with whichever group accounts for the largest part of the measured quantity, however large that group's gains and however small its number. A scheme that transfers a large sum to a minority raises the total while leaving the median household, and often the large majority of households, exactly where it was or slightly worse off. The total is not wrong; it answers a different question, namely how much in all was distributed or produced. Questions about whether things improved for the people the policy was aimed at require the distribution, and usually the median or the spread, rather than the sum.

questions.explanation: The item tests why a rising total says nothing about the typical household, since the total is dominated by whoever gained most. Answering questions about household outcomes requires the distribution rather than the sum.
questions.hint: Ask which group drives the total.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Read a source about measure choice and gaming

stimulus.body: A survey annotation records that a department's target for the year was the number of cases closed, that the number of open cases rose by a third, and that the department reported its target as met in full. The annotation adds that the target had not changed in five years.

questions.stem: According to the annotation, what does the record show about the single measure of success?

options.text: The department's performance was strong, since the target was met in full
options.misconception: treats a met closure target as strong performance

options.text: The measure was met while the underlying problem grew, because closing cases is easier to increase than reducing the backlog
The annotation is wrong, since a rising backlog and a met target cannot occur together
options.misconception: believes a met target and a growing backlog cannot coexist

options.text: The target was badly set, since no measure of closure is ever adequate on its own
options.misconception: blames the choice of target rather than the single measure

questions.explanation: The record shows the classic effect of a single measure: closing cases is directly within the department's control, so the count rises while the backlog grows, and the reported success is accurate about the target and misleading about the service. The pairing of the measures, not the honesty of the reporting, is the problem.
questions.hint: Ask what the department could most easily increase.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the agenda distinction to a media case

stimulus.body: A field note records that a story about a water company ran on the front of every paper for a fortnight, that ministers discussed the issue publicly, and that the company's published plan of investment contained nothing new for the area concerned. The note asks the cartographer to record where the issue sat.

questions.stem: According to the field note, what does the record support?

options.text: The issue had no political salience, since the investment plan did not change
options.misconception: reads absence from the plan as absence of salience

options.text: The issue entered the official agenda, since ministers discussed it publicly
options.misconception: takes ministerial discussion as entry to the agenda

options.text: The issue reached high attention and ministerial discussion but not the official agenda of planned work
The issue was a press invention, since the coverage outran the evidence
options.misconception: treats press attention as an invented problem

questions.explanation: Press coverage and ministerial discussion are measures of attention and salience, while the published investment plan is the record of the official agenda, and the note shows the issue absent from it. Public discussion does not by itself move anything onto the schedule.
questions.hint: Separate attention measures from the agenda record.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Delivery left out of a promise
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a delivery gap is being concealed
questions.stem: A programme's report lists only announcements, no deliveries, and no missed targets. Which judgement is most defensible?

options.text: The report is adequate, since targets are set by the programme itself
options.misconception: accepts a self-set target as sufficient evidence

options.text: The report shows the programme was active, since announcements prove work was done
options.misconception: treats announcements as proof that work was done

options.text: The report shows the programme failed, since no deliveries are listed
options.misconception: reads missing deliveries as proof the programme failed

options.text: The report cannot support any claim about results, since it omits the evidence that would show whether commitments were met

questions.explanation: Announcements show only that promises were made, and without deliveries or missed targets the reader cannot tell whether anything was achieved, so no claim about results follows from the report. Neither activity nor failure can be inferred from a list of intentions.
questions.hint: Ask what the report gives no evidence about.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the consequences of a particular sequencing choice
questions.stem: A planning sheet proposes to launch a new payment system on the busiest day of the year so that the publicity is greatest.

options.text: Launching on the busiest day spreads the disruption widely, which is fairer to all users
options.misconception: treats widely spread disruption as fair to all users

options.text: Publicity is at its peak while staff and users are least able to absorb the change, so the sequence raises failure risk
The sequence is harmless, since the system is the same on every day of the year
options.misconception: believes daily demand and staffing never change

options.text: Launching first is better, since later changes cannot be blamed on the launch
options.misconception: believes going first shields a scheme from later blame

questions.explanation: Implementation steps are sequenced against the capacity available to absorb them, so choosing the peak of the year for a change puts the new system under the heaviest load and the fewest staff able to support it. The publicity benefit does not offset the risk to the change itself.
questions.hint: Ask what the load and the staffing look like that day.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how compensation can protect a policy from opposition
questions.stem: Explain, for the projection note, why compensating those who lose from a change can be what allows the change to happen at all.

answer.exemplar: A change is blocked by those who bear its costs, so a policy that compensates them converts a contest over the whole change into a contest over the compensation. Where the compensation is credible, large enough to matter and offered to every loser on the same terms, the affected group has a reason to support rather than oppose, because their position is protected. That removes the most organised opposition and can leave a measure that would otherwise have been defeated intact. The compensation is therefore not a side payment attached to a settled policy but part of the design that makes the policy possible.

questions.explanation: The item tests that compensation works by changing the position of the affected group, not by softening the change itself. A credible offer of protection converts opponents into parties to the bargain.
questions.hint: Ask what compensation does to the losers' incentives.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish what each efficacy measure captures

stimulus.body: A survey annotation records two items. The first asks whether the respondent believes their own complaints reach the people who decide. The second asks whether the respondent believes those people listen to people like them. The annotation notes that the two items move in opposite directions in every wave of the survey.

questions.stem: According to the annotation, what do the two items measure?

options.text: The first measures external efficacy and the second internal efficacy
options.misconception: reverses the internal and external efficacy of the items

options.text: Both items measure the same belief, so the opposite movement shows the survey is faulty
options.misconception: treats opposite movement of one belief as a survey fault

options.text: The first measures internal efficacy and the second external efficacy, and the two are moving apart
The first measures satisfaction with services and the second measures trust in them
options.misconception: confuses efficacy forms with service satisfaction and trust

questions.explanation: The first item asks about the respondent's own capacity to reach decision-makers, which is internal efficacy, and the second asks about the system's responsiveness, which is external efficacy. Their opposite movement across waves is a substantive finding about growing personal confidence alongside declining faith in the system's listening.
questions.hint: Ask which one is about the person and which about the system.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Design a diagnostic that isolates a failing dimension

stimulus.body: A field note describes a programme with an acceptable overall grade whose components are cost, coverage, speed and satisfaction. The note records that coverage rose steadily, satisfaction fell steadily, and that the programme's own report listed only the overall grade and the coverage figure.

questions.stem: What should the programme's next report do, on the evidence in the field note?

options.text: Drop satisfaction from the grade entirely, since one weak component spoils the whole measure
options.misconception: believes a failing component should be dropped, not shown

options.text: Publish only the overall grade, since the components are too detailed for a public report
options.misconception: believes components are too detailed for a public report

options.text: Publish only satisfaction, since a single clear figure is easier for the public to understand
options.misconception: believes one clear figure can replace the set of components

options.text: Publish all four components alongside the overall grade, so the falling satisfaction cannot be hidden by rising coverage

questions.explanation: Reporting all the components alongside the composite makes the falling satisfaction visible instead of letting rising coverage mask it, which is the whole purpose of disaggregating a score. Publishing a single component would merely move the concealment to a different figure.
questions.hint: Make every component visible, not just the flattering ones.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Synthesise a distributional reading of a policy
questions.stem: A subsidy raises incomes for the poorest tenth and cuts a charge that only the richest tenth paid. How should this be mapped?

options.text: One distribution of the total subsidy, divided equally across the whole population
options.misconception: pools both components into one equal-share distribution

options.text: Two separate distributions, one for the gain and one for the avoided cost, each read against who receives it
One distribution showing the poorest tenth as winners and the richest tenth as losers
options.misconception: reads a charge cut as a loss to those who paid it

options.text: No distribution, since the two parts cancel out and the policy has no net effect
options.misconception: believes benefits and costs cancel, so nothing to map

questions.explanation: The two components reach different groups through different routes, so each has its own distribution and its own incidence, and reading them together as one figure or as a cancellation loses both. Mapping them separately is what lets the reader see who actually benefits and who actually pays.
questions.hint: Ask who is in each of the two groups.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Recall why one indicator cannot serve several aims
questions.stem: A legend drafted for the projected sheet needs a one-line rule for choosing how success is recorded.

options.text: Use the measure that is easiest to collect, since consistency matters more than coverage
options.misconception: believes ease of collection outranks covering every aim

options.text: Use the single most visible measure, since the public will not read anything longer
options.misconception: believes visibility should outweigh coverage of the aims

options.text: Use a separate measure for each distinct aim, so that no single figure has to stand for all of them
Use a weighted average, since one number is what comparisons require
options.misconception: believes a weighted average keeps what each aim promised

questions.explanation: Each aim needs its own measure, because a single figure necessarily leaves out some of what the policy promised and creates room for success on one aim to offset failure on another. Convenience, visibility and comparability all favour one number, and all three lose the substance of the policy.
questions.hint: One aim, one measure.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a crowded agenda can absorb attention
questions.stem: Explain, for the projection note, why an issue attracting a great deal of public attention may still not reach the official agenda.

answer.exemplar: An official agenda reflects what officials can take on, not what the public is talking about, and capacity is fixed for a period while attention is not. When many issues are already competing for a limited number of slots, the marginal issue is crowded out even if its public interest is high, and officials will normally prioritise an issue that fits an existing commitment, an established programme or a bargain already struck with partners. Attention raises the pressure to act, but the decision to act is taken against these institutional commitments and against what is already scheduled, so an issue can be widely discussed and still wait.

questions.explanation: The item tests the capacity constraint behind the agenda, since attention cannot create slots in a fixed schedule. Officials also prefer issues that fit commitments they have already made.
questions.hint: Ask what limits the number of things that can be scheduled.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Delivery left out of a promise
questions.learningObjective: Assess the credibility implications of a delivery gap

stimulus.body: A survey annotation records that a body has published five funding commitments in three years, that none of the five reached full delivery, and that the sixth commitment was announced with a larger figure and a shorter timetable. It records that the sixth announcement was welcomed enthusiastically in the correspondence received.

questions.stem: According to the annotation, what does the pattern do to the credibility of future commitments?

options.text: The record shows the body has more resources now, since larger commitments require them
options.misconception: reads a record of failure as evidence of greater resources

options.text: The response to the sixth announcement shows credibility has been rebuilt by the larger figure
options.misconception: treats warm correspondence as proof of restored credibility

options.text: Credibility is unaffected, since each commitment is judged on its own merits
options.misconception: believes each commitment is judged without its record

options.text: A long record of undelivered promises should reduce the credibility of the new commitment, whatever the response to it

questions.explanation: Credibility is built from a record, so five undelivered commitments give observers a basis for discounting the sixth whatever they say in response at the time. The correspondence measures present mood rather than the standing evidence about performance.
questions.hint: Ask what a long record of non-delivery does to the next promise.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a sequencing claim against alternatives
questions.stem: A review concludes that the scheme failed because one early decision was badly timed. Which qualification is most defensible?

options.text: The conclusion is complete, since the earliest decision determines the outcome of a scheme
options.misconception: believes the earliest decision alone settles the outcome

options.text: The conclusion is plausible, since early decisions constrain later ones, but it needs evidence that a different order would have performed better
The conclusion is wrong, since ordering has no effect on implementation results
options.misconception: denies that order affects implementation results at all

options.text: The conclusion is beside the point, since failure is always caused by funding rather than by order
options.misconception: believes funding is always the cause of scheme failure

questions.explanation: Path dependence makes early decisions consequential, so the conclusion is plausible, but a causal claim also requires showing that a different sequence would have produced a better result, since many other differences may explain the failure. A verdict on the earliest decision alone is not a demonstration of cause.
questions.hint: Ask what evidence would be needed to show the order caused it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the winners and losers created by a change
questions.stem: A mapping exercise asks which groups gain and which lose when a free bus pass is given to people over seventy and to students, with the fare removed for everyone else.

options.text: Only the operator loses, since the pass costs it nothing to issue
options.misconception: believes the pass itself costs the operator nothing to issue

options.text: Everyone gains, since the fare has been removed for all passengers
options.misconception: treats a fare removal as a benefit to every rider

options.text: Over-seventies and students gain the pass, and other riders lose the revenue that funded the service
The fare removal is a separate policy, so it has no bearing on this distribution
options.misconception: treats the fare removal as outside this distribution

questions.explanation: The pass gives a free journey to two named groups, while removing the fare from the rest removes the revenue that paid for the service, so other riders and the operator bear the cost. Treating a removal as a benefit to everyone ignores that a fare is a payment, not a charge for nothing.
questions.hint: Ask who used to pay the fare.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a survey can show rising participation with falling trust
questions.stem: Explain, for the projection note, how it is possible for political participation to rise while belief that the system responds falls.

answer.exemplar: Participation and belief in responsiveness measure different things, so they can move apart without any inconsistency. Participation reflects the cost and the appeal of acting, and campaigns, disputes and procedural changes can make acting easier or more rewarding even while government is no more responsive than before. External efficacy reflects a separate judgement about whether the system answers, and that judgement falls when people conclude that their efforts produced talk rather than change. In such a case each campaign becomes an occasion for discovering that the system does not answer, so participation rises while confidence in its responsiveness falls.

questions.explanation: The item tests why rising activity can coexist with declining belief in the system's responsiveness, since the two concern the cost of acting and the expected payoff. Each campaign can supply fresh evidence of non-response.
questions.hint: Ask what each trend is actually measuring.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why identifying the failing dimension matters for remedy
questions.stem: Explain, for the projection note, why isolating which dimension failed matters more than the overall grade.

answer.exemplar: The overall grade tells a reader that the programme is middling or weak, but it does not say what to do, because different remedies follow from different failures. A programme with high cost and poor take-up needs a cheaper design and a lower barrier to claiming, while a programme with good take-up and poor reliability needs a different fix, and the two require different money, staff and time. The components also explain why the overall grade moved, since a change in the grade comes from a change in a part. Working from the components turns a judgement into a set of specific decisions.

questions.explanation: The item tests why the grade alone cannot guide action, because remedies follow from the specific failing component. Components also explain what actually moved the total.
questions.hint: Ask what you would do differently for each component.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess a distributional claim against its data

stimulus.body: A field note records that a payment scheme raised the incomes of its recipients by a third on average and that the average payment across all households, including those outside the scheme, rose by two per cent. The note also records that the recipients were drawn from the poorest fifth of households.

questions.stem: According to the note, which reading of the distributional effect is best supported?

options.text: A regressive effect, since the recipients received less than the average household
options.misconception: mistakes a gain above average for a regressive effect

options.text: A small universal gain, since the average payment rose by only two per cent
options.misconception: reads the overall average as the gain each household got

options.text: No distributional effect, since the change is smaller than two per cent for most households
options.misconception: believes a small average implies no distributional effect

options.text: A large concentrated gain and a small spread gain, so the scheme is progressive in distribution

questions.explanation: The recipients, drawn from the poorest fifth, gained a third each while the gain spread across all households averaged two per cent, so the benefit is concentrated on the poorest group and the average figure describes only the small part that reached everyone else. The overall percentage is not the measure of who gained.
questions.hint: Ask where the gain was concentrated.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a single measure changes behaviour
questions.stem: Explain, for the projection note, how the choice of a single success measure shapes the behaviour of the people being measured.

answer.exemplar: A measure becomes a target, and a target becomes an instruction about what to do. Once the department's reported success depends on a single figure, the rational response is to move that figure, which usually means shifting effort towards whatever the figure records and away from whatever it ignores. If the figure counts cases closed, staff close cases; if it counts cases opened, staff open them; if it counts waiting time, the quickest improvement comes from reclassifying the long waiters rather than from treating them. The behaviour is not dishonest in the usual sense, since each change is locally defensible, but the aggregate outcome can be worse while the reported measure improves.

questions.explanation: The item tests the mechanism by which a measure redirects effort, so the reported figure can improve while the underlying service does not. The distortion is a predictable response to the incentive, not an exception to it.
questions.hint: Ask what the people being measured can do to the number.

questions.learningObjective: Synthesise the relationship between attention and agenda change
questions.stem: An issue dominates public attention for a month and then leaves the official agenda untouched. Which account best explains this outcome?

options.text: Attention was ignored entirely, since officials do not notice public concerns
options.misconception: believes officials never notice public concerns at all

options.text: Attention created pressure but no vehicle carried it onto the schedule, so the attention passed without a decision
The issue was resolved during the month, which is why it left the agenda
options.misconception: reads leaving the agenda as evidence the issue was resolved

options.text: The official agenda follows attention closely, so the schedule must have been revised
options.misconception: believes the official agenda automatically follows attention

questions.explanation: Attention is a pressure that has to be converted by something, such as a champion inside the organisation, a commitment already made to an interest, or a decision to make the issue a priority, and in this case no such vehicle existed. Pressure without a vehicle dissipates, and the agenda returns to what was already scheduled.
questions.hint: Ask what would have had to carry the issue onto the schedule.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Delivery left out of a promise
questions.learningObjective: Explain why delivery and announcement are different achievements
questions.stem: A survey legend must mark two kinds of government commitment on the projected sheet.

options.text: An announcement and a ceremony, since both are public events worth recording
options.misconception: records public events rather than outcomes for the public

options.text: A promise made and a promise broken, since only failure is worth mapping
options.misconception: believes only broken promises are worth recording

options.text: A promise made and a promise met, since only the second shows the public what was achieved
A plan and a budget, since both are the machinery of delivery
options.misconception: records inputs like plans and budgets instead of outcomes

questions.explanation: An announcement records an intention and a delivery records an outcome, and only the second speaks to what the public received, so the two belong in separate categories on any record of achievement. The other pairings mix up inputs and outputs or ignore the outcomes entirely.
questions.hint: One is an intention, the other is an outcome.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Recall why the order of implementation steps matters
questions.stem: The cartographer's introduction asks the reader to accept that implementation steps are not interchangeable. Which statement carries that idea best?

options.text: Sequencing matters only for large schemes, since small ones have too few steps
options.misconception: believes sequencing matters only for large schemes

options.text: Steps can be swapped freely, since a scheme succeeds or fails on its design alone
options.misconception: believes implementation steps can be reordered freely

options.text: Only the first step matters, since the rest are routine and predictable
options.misconception: believes later steps are routine and only the first matters

options.text: Each step changes the conditions the next step meets, so the sequence can determine whether the scheme works

questions.explanation: Implementation is sequential and path dependent because each step alters the state the following step encounters, so the same set of steps arranged differently can produce different results. Treating steps as interchangeable removes the very mechanism that makes order matter.
questions.hint: Ask what each step leaves behind for the next.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a change without compensation can be defeated

stimulus.body: A field note records a change that produced large savings, no compensation for those affected, and a long period of organised objection during which the measure was not brought forward. A second change, with modest compensation for a smaller group, was passed without sustained objection.

questions.stem: What does the field note suggest about why the second change passed?

options.text: The second change was smaller, since size determines whether objections succeed
options.misconception: credits the smaller size of the change for its passage

options.text: Compensation removed the organised opposition that had blocked the first change
The second change had better publicity, since publicity defeats organised objection
options.misconception: credits better publicity for defeating organised opposition

options.text: The second change passed because organised groups rarely oppose anything
options.misconception: believes organised groups rarely oppose policy changes

questions.explanation: In the first case the affected group had a clear interest in resisting and nothing to lose by resisting, while in the second the compensation removed that interest, so the opposition had no reason to organise. The pattern points to the effect of compensation on incentives.
questions.hint: Ask what the second group gained from objecting.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Recall what external efficacy measures

stimulus.body: A survey annotation records an item asking whether the respondent believes that ordinary people have a say in the decisions taken by the national government, and notes that it is often confused with an item asking whether the respondent feels personally able to take part.

questions.stem: According to the annotation, what does the first item measure?

options.text: Institutional trust, since it concerns how the national government is regarded
options.misconception: confuses system responsiveness with trust in the government

options.text: Internal efficacy, since it concerns the citizen's own capacity to act
options.misconception: confuses system responsiveness with personal capacity to act

options.text: External efficacy, since it concerns whether the political system responds to ordinary citizens
Civic knowledge, since it concerns what the respondent knows about government
options.misconception: confuses responsiveness with the respondent's own knowledge

questions.explanation: The item asks whether the system as a whole gives ordinary citizens a say, which is the system-level belief that defines external efficacy, and it is distinct from the citizen-level belief about personal capacity in the second item. It measures a perceived responsiveness, not a judgement about the government's honesty or the respondent's knowledge.
questions.hint: Ask whether the item is about the system or the person.

questions.learningObjective: Synthesise a diagnosis using disaggregated measures

options.text: The scheme should be stopped, since a falling satisfaction score invalidates the rest
options.misconception: believes one weak component invalidates the whole scheme

options.text: The scheme is performing well on the aims that matter and the satisfaction figure is noise
options.misconception: dismisses the failing satisfaction component as noise

options.text: The overall grade must be wrong, since three good dimensions should produce a good grade
options.misconception: believes three good components must produce a good grade

options.text: The cost, speed and coverage gains are offsetting a deteriorating satisfaction score, so the weak dimension is service quality

questions.explanation: Disaggregating the grade shows that the strong dimensions on cost, speed and coverage are offsetting a service quality score that is declining, and that is the dimension needing attention. questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the incidence of a policy on a named group
questions.stem: A mapping sheet asks who bears the cost when a road is widened by taking land from one set of houses and paying compensation to their owners.

options.text: The road users, since every journey is marginally faster after the widening
options.misconception: counts the beneficiaries of speed as those bearing the cost

options.text: The households that lose their land, though compensation partly offsets what they give up
The local authority, since it has to find the money for the compensation
options.misconception: treats the payer of compensation as the bearer of incidence

options.text: Nobody, since compensation means the scheme is costless to those affected
options.misconception: believes compensation leaves the affected households whole

questions.explanation: The incidence falls on the households whose land is taken, since the loss of a home is not fully offset by a payment, even though compensation softens it. The speed benefit for road users and the authority's own expenditure are separate matters and are not the cost being asked about.
questions.hint: Ask who gives up what the scheme is built on.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a balanced set of measures is hard to adopt
questions.stem: Explain, for the projection note, why agencies so often retain a single headline measure even after the case for several is well understood.

answer.exemplar: Several measures are harder to use in a decision because they must be read together and weighed, while one figure can be quoted, ranked and set as a target without interpretation. The single measure also serves institutional interests, since whoever controls the target controls what counts, and departments that had built reporting around one figure resist changing it. Reporting several measures spreads accountability across them, so a department can no longer be judged on the dimension it performs worst, and that prospect is a real obstacle to the change. Proving the case for better measurement is therefore not the same as getting it adopted.

questions.explanation: The item tests the practical reasons a single measure survives despite its known defects, which lie in ease of use and in who controls the target. Without those obstacles the case for several measures would settle quickly.
questions.hint: Ask who benefits from the existing arrangement.

options.misconception: reads silence in the record as private settlement

options.text: Attention produced influence, since the application would otherwise have been changed
options.misconception: assumes attention forces a decision change

options.text: Attention rose sharply and then faded, while the decision proceeded as if nothing had happened
The correspondence figure is unreliable, since only opponents write in about quarries
options.misconception: treats correspondence as a record of opponents only

questions.explanation: The note records a sharp rise in attention, its disappearance without any announced decision, and a decision taken on the original timetable, so attention rose and faded without producing influence. Coverage volume measures visibility, not the capacity to change a decision.
questions.hint: Compare the correspondence with the decision.

options.misconception: believes a summary figure is an adequate record

options.misconception: equates announcement counts with real commitment

questions.learningObjective: Recall that every policy creates identifiable winners and losers
questions.stem: A cartographer's note asks what every policy change produces for the people it affects, whether or not the change is described as a whole.

options.misconception: believes a change cannot reach outside the institution

options.misconception: assumes the state acts only for the common good

A measurable loss only, since gains are too diffuse to identify

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the consequences of falling external efficacy
questions.stem: Explain, for the projection note, why a fall in external efficacy can reduce participation even while internal efficacy stays high.

answer.exemplar: External efficacy is the expected payoff from acting, because it is the belief that the system will answer people like you. When that belief weakens, the rational calculation changes even if nothing has changed about the person's own ability to campaign or organise, so the cost of acting comes to outweigh a payoff that is no longer expected. Internal efficacy supplies the capacity and the confidence, which is why it can remain high while participation falls, and the gap between the two is where disengagement starts. Programmes that rely on enthusiasm alone therefore find that confidence is not enough without a visible route for it to be answered.

questions.explanation: The item tests why confidence in one's own capacity does not sustain action once the expected response disappears. The two beliefs enter the decision differently, one as capability and one as payoff.
questions.hint: Ask what has changed about the calculation, not about the person.

options.misconception: treats the composite rating as proof of good performance

options.text: A uniform decline across all four measures, since complaints have doubled
options.misconception: generalises one rising complaint figure to every measure

options.text: A serious and growing failure on accessible vehicles, hidden by strong results elsewhere and by the weighting

The rating and the complaints are consistent once the components are examined.

options.misconception: believes the firm's choice of who to charge sets the burden

options.text: The buyers of the second product, since a fixed budget absorbs a price rise far less comfortably
Both groups equally, since the price rise is the same in both cases

options.misconception: believes hardship cannot be measured at all

options.text: The measure is well chosen, since reaching more households must mean less hardship
options.misconception: assumes more households reached means less hardship

The measure should be dropped in favour of spending, since spending is the real outcome
options.misconception: treats spending rather than hardship as the real outcome

questions.explanation: Counting households reached records the extent of the programme's contact with people, which is not the same as the change in their circumstances, and a measure should be judged against the purpose it is used to serve. The mismatch does not make the count worthless, it makes it an incomplete answer to the question asked.
questions.hint: Compare the measure with the stated purpose.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Recall what the official agenda records
questions.stem: A glossary compiled for the projected sheet must define what an official agenda is.

options.text: The set of matters that have been legislated, once a bill has been introduced
options.misconception: confuses the agenda with what has already been legislated

options.text: The set of matters the public has raised most often in recent months
options.misconception: confuses the official agenda with public attention

options.text: The set of matters that the media have covered most heavily
options.misconception: confuses the official agenda with media coverage

options.text: The set of matters the government has decided to give priority and act on during a period

questions.explanation: An official agenda is the government's own set of priorities and scheduled commitments, which is a decision about what to do rather than a record of public or media interest. Legislation is one way an agenda item becomes visible, but an agenda exists well before any bill is introduced.
questions.hint: Ask who decided the matter belongs there.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Delivery left out of a promise
questions.learningObjective: Explain how delivery gaps accumulate into lost trust
questions.stem: Explain, for the projection note, how a series of small delivery gaps can damage trust in a body more than one large gap.

answer.exemplar: Trust is formed from repeated encounters rather than from a single verdict, so a body whose promises are met almost always is trusted differently from one whose promises are met often enough to be noticed. Small gaps are more corrosive than one large gap because each arrives with its own excuse and none of them on its own looks significant, so they accumulate as a pattern of unreliability rather than as a single betrayal. A large gap produces shock and may produce anger, which is still attention, while small gaps produce a quiet expectation that nothing much will happen, and that expectation is what stops people bothering to engage at all.

questions.explanation: The item tests why repeated minor failures can be more damaging than a single obvious one, since they build an expectation of futility rather than provoking a reaction. The mechanism is accumulation through repetition.
questions.hint: Ask what a pattern of small gaps teaches people to expect.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why early decisions are more costly to revisit

stimulus.body: A field note describes a scheme whose first year enrolled only applicants from one district because the enrolment form had only been translated into one language. It records that by the second year the administration had been restructured around that pattern and that opening enrolment to others would now require renegotiating agreements with three external partners.

questions.stem: According to the field note, why is it now harder to correct the first year's enrolment pattern?

options.text: The translation of the enrolment form is a one-off task that cannot be repeated
options.misconception: treats a one-off translation as the lasting obstacle

options.text: The early decision has been built into later arrangements, so correcting it now would unsettle commitments made in reliance on it
The second year cannot change anything the first year decided, since decisions cannot be reviewed
options.misconception: believes decisions can never be reviewed or changed

options.text: The external partners have no legal power to object to a change in enrolment
options.misconception: assumes partners lack any right to object to a change

questions.explanation: Because the first year's pattern was built into the structure and the agreements formed on the basis of it, changing it now would unsettle commitments that were made in reliance on the original decision. The difficulty is a consequence of accumulated dependence, not of an inability to review anything.
questions.hint: Ask what was later built on the first decision.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how targeted benefits build a political constituency
questions.stem: Explain, for the projection note, why concentrating a policy's benefits on a small organised group tends to protect the policy in later years.

answer.exemplar: A policy's durability rests on who has an interest in keeping it, and a concentrated benefit produces a small but reliable constituency. The recipients of a focused benefit know exactly what they are getting, they can recognise threats to it, and they can organise faster than a diffuse group with a much larger but weaker interest. When the policy is later reviewed, that group is present, informed and organised, while the many who paid for it are dispersed and often unaware that a review is happening. The policy then survives on the strength of a minority's concentrated interest rather than the majority's diffuse approval.

questions.explanation: The item tests why concentrated benefits create an effective constituency, since the recipients are identifiable, organised and attentive to threats. Durability then follows the interest rather than the numbers.
questions.hint: Ask who knows what they are getting and can organise.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a programme that raises participation without raising influence
questions.stem: A programme raises meeting attendance sharply, and a survey afterwards shows confidence in one's own voice rose while belief that the council answers citizens fell. Which appraisal is best founded?

options.text: The programme failed, since it did not raise belief that the council listens
options.misconception: judges the programme only by external efficacy

options.text: The programme succeeded, since attendance and confidence are the outcomes that matter
options.misconception: treats participation alone as proof of programme success

options.text: The programme raised capacity and participation while leaving responsiveness untouched, so it addressed the wrong constraint
The results are contradictory and so the survey should be repeated before anything is concluded
options.misconception: treats two separate measures as a contradiction

questions.explanation: The programme raised the capacity and willingness to take part, which is the internal side, while leaving external efficacy where it was or lower, so it removed one obstacle and left the binding one in place. Nothing in the results is contradictory, since the two measures capture separate beliefs.
questions.hint: Ask which constraint the programme removed and which it left.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Recall why a composite must be broken into parts
questions.stem: A legend entry explains how composite grades should be read on the projected sheet.

options.text: A composite should be replaced by its highest component, since that reflects the real strength
options.misconception: takes the best component as the true measure of performance

options.text: A composite is the most reliable figure available, since it combines everything
options.misconception: assumes a combined figure is more reliable than its parts

options.text: A composite is only useful for ranking, so it says nothing about any single aspect
options.misconception: believes a composite says nothing about its components

options.text: A composite hides the components, so the components should always be read alongside it

questions.explanation: A composite is useful for summarising but necessarily conceals the components, and one weak component can be offset by others, so the components must be published with it. The alternative that treats the composite as sufficient repeats the concealment the note warns about.
questions.hint: Ask what the total cannot show.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an apparent gain can hide a loss elsewhere
questions.stem: Explain, for the projection note, how a change that produces a clear gain for one group can leave another group worse off while the overall figure improves.

answer.exemplar: An overall figure records the sum of gains and losses, so a large gain can outweigh a smaller loss and produce an improvement in the total while one group is worse off than before. Because the total is the only published number, the loss is not visible and the affected group may have no reason to expect any remedy. This is why a change presented as an improvement can be experienced as a loss by the people whose costs rise, and why the map of a policy's effects has to be drawn group by group rather than as a single shaded region representing the whole. The label on the aggregate cannot substitute for that map.

questions.explanation: The item tests that improvement in the total does not exclude a group being worse off, since the total is a net figure. Mapping the effects group by group is what exposes the loss.
questions.hint: Ask what the total has swallowed up.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Read a source on the limits of headline success figures

stimulus.body: A survey annotation records that a scheme reports success by counting how many participants finished a course, that the count has risen each year, and that the number of participants reporting that the course changed what they do at work has stayed flat. It notes that the scheme is funded according to the completion count.

questions.stem: According to the annotation, what does the source show?

options.text: The scheme is succeeding on the outcome that matters, since completions always precede change
options.misconception: assumes completions always lead to real change

options.text: The funded measure and the outcome measure have diverged, and the funding arrangement keeps the divergence stable
The scheme is failing, since the outcome figure has not improved
options.misconception: reads a flat outcome figure as outright failure

options.text: The annotation shows the annotation itself is biased, since a rise in completions must mean a rise in change
options.misconception: treats a rise in completions as proof of rising change

questions.explanation: Completion counts are rising while reported effects are flat, so the measure that is funded has drifted away from the outcome that was intended, and the funding rule locks in that arrangement by rewarding completions. Neither success nor failure follows from the completion count alone.
questions.hint: Compare the funded measure with the outcome measure.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Conclude an analysis of attention and priority

stimulus.body: A field note records that the issue with the highest public attention in every year for a decade has never appeared in any published programme of work, while a low-salience issue mentioned in a single interview has been funded for four consecutive years. The note observes that the second issue was included in a commitment given to a partner body.

questions.stem: What does the field note best support?

options.text: Attention has no relationship with priority in any case whatsoever
options.misconception: believes attention and priority are never connected

options.text: The high-salience issue was rejected because the public was not sufficiently organised
options.misconception: explains rejection by a lack of public organisation

options.text: Priority is set by commitments and capacity rather than by public attention, since the funded issue is sustained by an existing commitment
The note shows public attention is actively harmful to issues that do get funded
options.misconception: believes public attention harms the issues it reaches

questions.explanation: The sustained funding of a low-salience issue is explained by the commitment already given to a partner body, which shows the official agenda being driven by existing obligations and capacity rather than by attention. The note does not support a claim that attention is irrelevant, only that it did not decide these cases.
questions.hint: Ask what explains the sustained funding.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Weigh a sequencing judgement against the whole process
questions.stem: A scheme's first year delivered nothing because the announcement was made before the money was secured, and the second year delivered everything once the funding and systems were ready. Which reading is most defensible?

options.text: The scheme is now secure, since the second year delivered everything and the sequence is settled
options.misconception: assumes one good year settles the scheme's security

options.text: The first year failed because the announcement was public, so publicity is what caused the failure
options.misconception: blames publicity rather than the order of the steps

options.text: The scheme was well designed and merely unlucky, since a sound design should survive a bad first year
options.misconception: blames luck and assumes good design resists any bad year

options.text: The failure came from committing publicly before securing the means, and the recovery came from putting the resources and systems first

questions.explanation: The sequence in the first year committed the scheme publicly before the means to deliver existed, which is what produced the empty year, and reversing that order in the second year is what produced the delivery. The reading identifies the ordering rule rather than blaming publicity or bad luck.
questions.hint: Ask what changed between the two years.
